title: BJP and Akali Dal reunite for 2027 Punjab elections after six-year split
summary: The BJP and the Shiromani Akali Dal have formally revived their alliance for the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections, with the Akali Dal as senior partner and the chief minister's post going to the SAD, Union Home Minister Amit Shah announced in New Delhi on Tuesday.
content:
India's two oldest National Democratic Alliance partners are back together. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) on Tuesday formally revived their alliance for the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections, ending a six-year separation that began over the Centre's now-repealed farm laws.

The announcement was made by Union Home Minister Amit Shah at a joint press conference at the BJP headquarters in New Delhi, flanked by BJP national president Nitin Nabin and SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal. According to [The Economic Times](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/elections/assembly-elections/punjab/amit-shah-alliance-sukhbir-singh-badal/articleshow/136122797.cms), Shah welcomed the Akali Dal back into the NDA, declaring that with its return the alliance was complete.

The timing was deliberate. The pact was unveiled on Gurpurab, the birth anniversary of Guru Nanak Dev, after months of quiet negotiations between leaders of the two parties, both weakened by consecutive electoral defeats in Punjab. Shah described the partnership as a natural alliance, recalling ties that stretch back to the era of former prime ministers Atal Bihari Vajpayee and L.K. Advani, and to the leadership of former Punjab chief minister Parkash Singh Badal, under whom the two parties first joined hands in 1996 following the Moga Declaration.

The deal settles the question that had hung over the reunion for months: who leads. Shah said the Akali Dal would play the role of the "Bade Bhai" — the elder brother — in Punjab, and that the chief minister would come from the SAD. The announcement effectively clears the way for Sukhbir Singh Badal to become the alliance's chief ministerial candidate. The two parties will contest all 117 Assembly seats together, with seat-sharing talks to follow.

Drugs will be the centrepiece of the campaign. Shah promised that an NDA government would make Punjab drug-free by December 31, 2029, and said the drug menace, law and order, corruption and the state's economic difficulties would form the core of the election agenda. The pledge speaks directly to the crisis that has dominated Punjab's politics for a decade: a narcotics trade that successive governments have promised to end and none has.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi welcomed the tie-up the same evening, calling it a "natural alliance" that would ensure pro-people governance and take Punjab to new heights of progress. Sukhbir Singh Badal, for his part, described the alliance as more than a political arrangement, calling it a natural bond of brotherhood formed in the interest of Punjab.

The reunion redraws the map of the 2027 contest. Punjab now looks set for a four-cornered fight: the ruling Aam Aadmi Party seeking a second term, the Congress attempting to regain ground, the revived BJP-Akali Dal alliance, and Waris Punjab De, the organisation associated with jailed Lok Sabha MP Amritpal Singh, which has built its support around Panthic issues. It is a crowded field, and that is precisely why the arithmetic mattered. Analysts quoted by Mathrubhumi put the two parties' combined vote share at roughly 32 per cent — enough, in a split field, to turn a reunion of two weakened parties into a genuine contender.

Neither party comes to the table from strength, and both know it. The BJP has never won Punjab on its own, and its organisation in the state remains thin outside urban pockets. The SAD, once the dominant force in rural Punjab, has been out of power since 2017 and has watched its vote erode to the AAP and to new Panthic challengers. What each lacks, the other supplies: the BJP brings the Centre's resources and a national campaign machine; the SAD brings a rural Sikh base and a cadre the BJP has never built. That complementarity is the bet behind the reunion — and the reason the talks dragged on for months over who would be the senior partner.

The split they are repairing dates to September 2020, when the SAD walked out of the NDA in protest against the three farm laws, and its minister Harsimrat Kaur Badal resigned from the Union cabinet. The laws were repealed a year later, but the political damage lingered: the two parties fought the 2022 Assembly election separately and were both routed by the AAP. Tuesday's announcement closes that chapter, at least formally.

What happens next will test whether the reunion is more than a press conference. Seat-sharing negotiations begin now, and the two sides must divide 117 constituencies without reopening old wounds — the SAD will expect the lion's share, in keeping with its senior-partner status, while the BJP will want enough seats to justify its investment. The next major event is in Moga on December 8, when Modi is scheduled to attend a gathering marking the birth anniversary of Parkash Singh Badal, the architect of the original alliance. It will be the first joint public outing of the reunited partners, and the first real measure of whether the old chemistry still works.

For Punjab's voters, the promise is familiar: a drug-free state, clean governance, development. The state has heard versions of it from every party that has sought its votes. What is new is the combination — the BJP's national weight behind the Akali Dal's regional roots — and the calendar. With the election still months away, the alliance has time to build a campaign, and time, too, for its contradictions to surface. The test will come not in New Delhi press conferences but in the villages and towns of Punjab, where the drug crisis Shah promised to end is lived every day.

The reunion also matters beyond Punjab. It restores to the NDA its oldest regional ally at a moment when the BJP is rebuilding alliances across states, and it signals that the party is willing to concede the senior role to a regional partner where the arithmetic demands it. The announcement comes as New Delhi juggles several diplomatic fronts at once, from [its delayed trade deal with Washington](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-us-trade-deal-signing-delayed-november-2026) to [a deepening security dialogue with Tokyo](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/india-japan-2-plus-2-dialogue-tokyo-november-2026) — a reminder that the government's domestic alliances and its foreign policy are moving on parallel tracks. Whether that concession buys victory in 2027 is the question the next year will answer. For now, the two parties that parted over the farm laws have found their way back to each other — on Gurpurab, in the capital, with the chief minister's chair already promised to the elder brother.
